Terrestrial organisms on Earth carry out their life activities while resisting gravity. In water, which is a kind of microgravity environment, cell walls extend more easily, and the elongation growth of plants is also promoted. On the basis of this result, the hypothesis was put forward that "if plants are grown in the microgravity of outer space, their cell walls will extend even more easily than in water, and their elongation growth will also be promoted further". Plants were therefore grown in orbit in space, and it was investigated how plant growth and the cell walls change in the microgravity environment of space. Control experiments under normal gravity were carried out on the ground.

However, inconsistent results were obtained: in the space environment, elongation growth was promoted, was inhibited, or was not affected. Behind this lay problems peculiar to outer space, such as 1) dry seeds take up water poorly under microgravity, 2) under microgravity it takes time for the temperature inside the plant growth container to become constant, and 3) ethylene accumulates inside the plant growth container.

The experimenters therefore carried out the experiment with devices and measures to solve these problems, and obtained results that supported the hypothesis based on the results of the ground experiments. ⑥ Ethylene-resistant plants were used.

⑦ An ethylene absorbent was placed inside the plant growth container.
